title: A Church That Turned from Idols
sum: Paul, Silvanus and Timothy greet a young church in Thessalonica and thank God for it. The church's faith works, its love toils and its hope endures (1:3). Paul is sure that God has chosen them, because the message came to them with power and the Holy Spirit and they welcomed it with joy, though it brought them trouble (1:4-6).

The chapter ends with a summary that may echo what new Gentile believers were first taught: they "turned away from idols to God, to serve a God who lives and is true, and to wait for his Son to come from the heavens," Jesus, who rescues from the coming anger (1:9-10). These verses set out the letter's themes: suffering and joy, Gentile converts who now belong to Israel's God, and the hope of Christ's coming.
readings: A thank-you note with a purpose

Read as a letter from a pastor who had to leave in a hurry, the chapter is praise with a purpose: it reminds the converts who they are and that what happened to them was real, at a time when neighbors were telling them otherwise.
A creed in miniature

Read as theology, 1:9-10 is one of the earliest summaries of Christian belief: one living and true God, his Son, raised from the dead, coming from heaven, rescuing from judgment. Later creeds grew from statements like this.

views.H: Thessalonica was the capital of Roman Macedonia (from 128 BC) and a free city (from 41 BC), a port on the Via Egnatia with its own city government; Acts calls its rulers politarchai (Acts 17:6, 8), a title also carved on the city's Vardar Gate, an inscription of the 2nd century AD. Converts who stopped worshiping the city's gods would have dropped out of festivals, trade-guild meals and family rites, which explains the "great trouble" (1:6).
views.C: Almost all scholars accept that Paul wrote this letter, and most date it about AD 50, which would make it the oldest surviving Christian writing; a few who date Galatians earlier dissent on the order. The difference between the letter (former idol worshipers, 1:9) and Acts 17 (synagogue converts) is a test case for how Acts relates to Paul's own letters.
views.L: The thanksgiving that begins in 1:2 is unusually long: it resumes at 2:13 and 3:9, so that some scholars see thanks as the frame of the whole first half (1:2-3:13). The triad of faith, love and hope (1:3) returns at 5:8.
views.J: "Turned from idols to the living and true God" is the language of Jewish teaching about Gentiles who come to Israel's God, and "the anger that is coming" is the prophets' day of the LORD. Paul speaks to Gentiles in Israel's terms without asking them to become Jews.
views.T: John Chrysostom preached a series of homilies on this letter. The churches have read 1:10 as a summary of the hope of the Creed: "he will come again to judge the living and the dead."

deep.b:
Most scholars date 1 Thessalonians to about AD 49-51, while Paul was at Corinth. The anchor is Acts 18: Paul stayed in Corinth "a year and six months" (Acts 18:11), and during that time he was brought before "Gallio ... proconsul of Achaia" (Acts 18:12). An inscription found at Delphi, a letter of the emperor Claudius written in AD 52 that calls Gallio "my friend and proconsul," is the anchor; from it Gallio's term is usually dated to about AD 51-52. Paul came to Corinth from Athens (Acts 18:1), and Timothy rejoined him there early in his stay (Acts 18:5), which is when this letter fits (3:6). The hearing before Gallio came later in the eighteen months, so the letter is dated before it: about AD 50, less than twenty years after Jesus' death. The date depends on the length of Gallio's term and on where in Paul's stay the hearing fell, which is why scholars give a range, AD 49-51.

That makes it, in the view of most scholars, the oldest surviving Christian writing and the earliest of Paul's letters. Those who dissent mostly date Galatians earlier, before the Jerusalem meeting of Acts 15. The late scribal note at the end of some manuscripts, "written from Athens" (see the variant at 5:28), is a guess from 3:1.

echoes: Acts 17:1-10; Acts 18:5; Jeremiah 10:10; 1 Corinthians 12:2; 1 Corinthians 13:13; Galatians 4:8-9; Acts 14:15; Acts 17:31; 2 Thessalonians 1:1-4

settings.to: The church at Thessalonica: mostly Gentile converts who had turned from the city's gods (1:9), with perhaps some Jews and God-fearers from the synagogue (Acts 17:4); working people for the most part (4:11), a few months old, meeting in houses, and under pressure from neighbors
settings.when: about AD 50, a few months after Paul, Silvanus and Timothy were forced out of the city (2:17; Acts 17:10), soon after Timothy came back with news (3:6); most scholars place Paul at Corinth when he wrote
settings.why: To open a letter that would be read aloud to the whole church (5:27) in the names of all three men they knew. The short greeting places the church "in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ," which tells the readers where they now belong after leaving the city's gods.

settings.to: The church at Thessalonica: mostly Gentile converts who had turned from the city's gods (1:9), with perhaps some Jews and God-fearers from the synagogue (Acts 17:4); working people for the most part (4:11), a few months old, meeting in houses, and under pressure from neighbors
settings.when: the same occasion: Timothy's good report (3:6) has just come
settings.why: To reassure new converts who had paid a price for their faith that their conversion was God's work: they were chosen (1:4), the message came with power (1:5), and their example was known far and wide (1:7-8). Knowing the audience changes the reading: this is not flattery but comfort for people whose neighbors scorned them, and a reminder of the hope (1:10) that the rest of the letter develops.

title: Like a Nurse, Like a Father
sum: Paul recalls how he and his partners lived in Thessalonica. After the beating at Philippi they came with courage, not trickery or greed, worked night and day to support themselves, and cared for the converts like a nurse and a father (2:1-12). The church received the message as the word of God, and it suffered from its own countrymen, as the churches in Judea suffered from "the Jews" (2:13-16).

Verses 14-16 are among the harshest Paul wrote, and later Christians used them against the Jewish people. This chapter page gives the case that a later hand added them and the replies, and how the verses have been read. The chapter ends with Paul's longing to come back, which Satan blocked, and his joy in the church as his crown at the Lord's coming (2:17-20).
readings: A defense
Read as an answer to critics, 2:1-12 replies to the charge that Paul was one more traveling teacher after money and fame, who fled and did not come back.
A model
Read as teaching by example, the same verses hold up the preachers' conduct as a pattern for the church: work, honesty, gentleness and care (compare 4:11-12; 5:12-14).

views.H: Traveling teachers were a common sight in Greek cities, and so was suspicion of them. Paul's handwork (2:9) set him apart from teachers who lived off patrons. The persecution of the Judean churches (2:14) is known from Galatians 1:22-23 and Acts 8 and 12.
views.C: The main question is 2:13-16. Some scholars, most fully Birger Pearson (1971), argued that the verses were added after AD 70; most now hold them to be Paul's (see the deep dive). Verse 7 has a famous textual problem: "infants" or "gentle" (see the variant).
views.L: Paul piles up family images: infants, a nurse, a father, an orphan (2:7, 11, 17). The thanksgiving starts again at 2:13. Verses 1-12 are carefully built from denials ("not ... but") that set true teachers against false ones.
views.J: Paul, a Jew, speaks here of Judean opponents in the words of Israel's own prophets ("killed the prophets," "fill up the measure"). Read in its setting this is a quarrel within the Jewish people about Jesus and about the mission to Gentiles. Read apart from that setting, as later Christians read it, it became a charge against all Jews. Many recent Jewish and Christian readers stress that Romans 9-11 is Paul's fuller word on his people.
views.T: Chrysostom read 2:7-8 as the model of the pastor's love. Since the Holocaust, the Catholic Church (Nostra Aetate 4, 1965) and many other churches have rejected the charge that the Jews as a people are guilty of Jesus' death, which verses like 2:15 were used to support.

deep.h: 1 Thessalonians 2:13-16: Paul, the Judeans, and later misuse
deep.b:
What the verses say. Paul says the Thessalonians suffered from their own countrymen as the Judean churches did from "the Jews, who killed the Lord Jesus as well as the prophets, and chased us out," who "do not please God" and stand "against all people," trying to stop the good news from reaching Gentiles; and "the anger has reached them in the end."

The case that a later hand added them. Since the middle of the 1800s (Timothy Brookins, 2021, as quoted by Wikipedia) some scholars have argued that these verses are not Paul's. The fullest case was made by Birger Pearson in the Harvard Theological Review (1971), with linguistic arguments added by Daryl Schmidt in the Journal of Biblical Literature (1983). Their reasons concern the passage's tone, its grammar and wording, and its timing: the sharp, general attack seems out of place in a Paul who calls himself a Jew and hopes that "all Israel will be saved" (Romans 11:26), and the past tense "the anger has reached them" seems to some to look back on the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70. Readers also note that "against all people" sounds like pagan slurs against Jews (compare Tacitus, Histories 5.5).

The replies. No known manuscript lacks the verses or places them elsewhere. Many point to the link between 2:13 and 2:14 and to the letter's rhetoric. They note that the passage fits the letter's own situation: the Thessalonians are suffering from their own countrymen (2:14), and "the anger that is coming" was already a theme at 1:10. Paul could be harsh about opponents elsewhere (Galatians 5:12; Philippians 3:2), though those words are aimed at rival teachers troubling his churches, not at Judean persecutors, so the parallel is only partial. Others point to the theme of Israel's killing of prophets in the Jewish Scriptures themselves (1 Kings 19:10; Nehemiah 9:26); and to possible events of the 40s, or the prophetic habit of speaking of coming judgment as already done. The commentaries of Andrew Johnson (2016), Nijay Gupta (2019) and Timothy Brookins (2021), and Matthew Jensen's review of the arguments (Currents in Biblical Research, 2019), all report that in the last thirty years most scholars have come to accept the verses as Paul's.

Who are "the Jews" here? The context is the persecution of the churches "in Judea," so many readers take Ioudaioi as "the Judeans" who opposed them, not the Jewish people as a whole. Frank Gilliard (1989) argued that the usual comma after "the Jews" gives a false picture, and that the clause should limit the words to the particular Jews who killed Jesus and persecuted the church. Others answer that Greek has no commas and the grammar allows either. The Plain keeps the comma, as most translations do, and leaves this note.

Later use. Christians later read 2:15 together with Matthew 27:25 as a charge that "the Jews" killed Christ, and the charge fed contempt and violence for centuries. The Catholic declaration Nostra Aetate (1965) says that Christ's passion "cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive, nor against the Jews of today," that "the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God," and that the Church "decries hatred, persecutions, displays of anti-Semitism, directed against Jews at any time and by anyone."
deep.refs: 1 Thessalonians 2:14-16; Romans 9:1-5; Romans 11:1; Romans 11:25-29; Matthew 27:25; Galatians 1:22-23; Acts 17:5; Galatians 5:12; Philippians 3:2; 1 Thessalonians 1:10

deep.title: Claude's theory: one family's quarrel, read by strangers
deep.b: Paul's words in 2:14-16 make most sense as words about the Judeans who, in his view, did to the churches of Judea what the Thessalonians' neighbors were doing to them, in a letter to Gentiles who had no stake in Jewish life. The trouble starts when Gentile readers, who did not belong to the family, overheard a family argument and took it as a verdict on the family. Paul himself seems to have seen the danger: in Romans 11:18 he warns Gentile believers, "do not boast over the branches." On this reading the passage needs no theory of a later addition, but it does need a note in every Bible, which is why this site gives it one. This overlaps with readings that stress the Jewish setting of Paul's quarrels, and it does not settle whether Paul's anger here was fair.

echoes: Acts 16:19-24; Acts 17:1-10; Acts 18:3; Jeremiah 11:20; Galatians 1:22-23; 1 Kings 19:10; Nehemiah 9:26; Matthew 23:31-32; Luke 11:49-50; Genesis 15:16; Romans 11:25-29; Romans 1:13; Philippians 4:1

settings.what: How the preachers lived among them
settings.by: Paul, speaking for himself, Silvanus and Timothy
settings.to: The church at Thessalonica: mostly Gentile converts who had turned from the city's gods (1:9), with perhaps some Jews and God-fearers from the synagogue (Acts 17:4); working people for the most part (4:11), a few months old, meeting in houses, and under pressure from neighbors
settings.when: the same occasion, written months after the preachers had to leave by night (Acts 17:10)
settings.why: To answer a doubt that could undo the church: had they been fooled by traveling teachers who took what they could and ran? Paul reminds them of what they saw: courage after Philippi, no flattery or greed, hard work so as to cost no one, and the care of a nurse and a father. Knowing the audience changes the reading: this is not self-praise but proof offered to converts whose neighbors mocked the men who had changed their lives.
views: Some in Thessalonica, perhaps outsiders or the converts' families, were attacking Paul's motives, and he answers them point by point.
Paul uses the familiar contrast between true and false teachers to give the church a model, without real critics in view.

settings.what: The word received, and the persecutors
settings.by: Paul and his co-workers (on the question whether a later hand added 2:13-16, see the deep dive)
settings.to: The church at Thessalonica: mostly Gentile converts who had turned from the city's gods (1:9), with perhaps some Jews and God-fearers from the synagogue (Acts 17:4); working people for the most part (4:11), a few months old, meeting in houses, and under pressure from neighbors
settings.why: To tell suffering converts that they are not alone: their pain from their own neighbors matches what the first churches in Judea suffered from theirs. The harsh words about the Judean persecutors are meant to set the Thessalonians' troubles in a larger story of God's word opposed and God's judgment coming. Knowing the audience matters greatly here: Gentile readers were hearing a Jew's words about a conflict among Jews, not a ruling on the Jewish people.
views: Most scholars today hold that Paul wrote the verses, in anger at those who opposed the mission to Gentiles.
Some scholars think a writer after AD 70 added them; no manuscript supports this.

settings.what: Torn away, Timothy sent, and the good news he brought
settings.by: Paul and his co-workers, with Paul speaking as "I" at 2:18 and 3:5
settings.to: The church at Thessalonica: mostly Gentile converts who had turned from the city's gods (1:9), with perhaps some Jews and God-fearers from the synagogue (Acts 17:4); working people for the most part (4:11), a few months old, meeting in houses, and under pressure from neighbors
settings.when: the same occasion, as Paul tells the story of the months since he left
settings.why: To explain why Paul had not come back, which the converts or their critics might take as proof that he did not care. He tells them how he tried to return, why he sent Timothy instead, and how Timothy's report brought him back to life. Knowing the audience changes the reading: the travel report is itself pastoral care for people who felt abandoned.

title: Timothy's Good News
sum: Unable to bear being cut off any longer, Paul stays alone in Athens and sends Timothy back to strengthen the church, fearing that the troubles he had warned them about might have broken their faith (3:1-5). Timothy returns with good news of their faith and love and their longing to see Paul, and Paul says, "For now we live, as long as you hold your ground in the Lord" (3:6-10).

The chapter ends in prayer: may God open a road back to them, make their love overflow, and make their hearts firm and holy at the coming of the Lord Jesus "with all his holy ones" (3:11-13). This prayer closes the first half of the letter and points to its two main themes: holy living (4:1-12) and the Lord's coming (4:13-5:11).
readings: A travel report
Read as history, the chapter is the best first-hand evidence for Paul's movements between Thessalonica, Athens and Corinth, and a check on the account in Acts 17-18.
A pastor's heart
Read as a letter of friendship, the chapter shows a missionary whose own well-being rises and falls with his converts: "now we live" (3:8).

views.H: Paul's route ran from Thessalonica to Berea and then by sea or road to Athens (Acts 17:10-15), and on to Corinth (Acts 18:1). Timothy's journeys between the cities explain the letter's occasion.
views.C: Acts and the letter differ on Timothy's movements (Acts 17:14-15; Acts 18:5). Scholars either combine the accounts or trust the letter as the first-hand source.
views.L: The prayer of 3:11-13 is a wish-prayer (optative verbs: "may God ... may the Lord"), which closes the long thanksgiving that began in 1:2 and introduces the themes of chapters 4 and 5.
views.J: "With all his holy ones" (3:13) echoes Zechariah 14:5, where the LORD comes with his heavenly host; Paul gives the coming of the LORD to the Lord Jesus.
views.T: The joint prayer to God the Father and the Lord Jesus with one singular verb (3:11) became a text in the debates about Christ's divinity.

echoes: Acts 17:14-16; Acts 18:1-5; Acts 14:22; Matthew 4:3; Zechariah 14:5; Matthew 16:27; Jude 1:14; Philippians 4:1; 2 Thessalonians 2:16-17

settings.to: The church at Thessalonica: mostly Gentile converts who had turned from the city's gods (1:9), with perhaps some Jews and God-fearers from the synagogue (Acts 17:4); working people for the most part (4:11), a few months old, meeting in houses, and under pressure from neighbors
settings.when: the same occasion, at the turn from thanksgiving to teaching
settings.why: To put into a prayer what the rest of the letter will teach: growing love (4:9-12) and holy, blameless hearts (4:1-8) at the Lord's coming (4:13-5:11). Spoken aloud in the church, it let the converts hear their own future prayed for. Knowing the audience changes the reading: for people who feared they had been forgotten, the prayer was proof that they were not.

title: Caught Up to Meet the Lord
sum: Chapter 4 turns from thanks to teaching. Paul reminds the church of what he taught in person: God's will is that they be holy, which begins with sexual conduct; each should gain control of his own "vessel" in holiness and not wrong a brother (4:1-8). They already love one another; they should aim to live quietly, mind their own affairs and work with their hands (4:9-12).

Then Paul answers a grief. Some members have died, and the living fear for them. Paul says the dead in Christ will rise first when the Lord comes down from heaven with a shout, an archangel's voice and God's trumpet, and then the living will be caught up with them in clouds to meet the Lord in the air, "And so we will be with the Lord always" (4:13-17). He writes it to comfort (4:18). These verses later became the main text for the teaching called the rapture.
readings: A word of comfort
Read in its setting, 4:13-18 is consolation for mourners. It answers one question (do the dead miss out?) and ends: "comfort one another with these words."
A map of the end

Read as prophecy, the passage is part of a larger picture assembled from Daniel, the Gospels, 1 Corinthians 15, 2 Thessalonians and Revelation. The churches have assembled that picture in very different ways (see the card).

views.H: Greek and Roman sexual customs allowed men much that Jewish law forbade. A Roman ruler's arrival in a city (parousia) was met by leading citizens going out to meet him (apantesis), which may color 4:15-17. Manual work (4:11) marks most of the converts as artisans and laborers.
views.C: Did Paul expect to be alive at the Lord's coming ("we who are alive," 4:15)? Many scholars say yes and see a development toward 2 Corinthians 5 and Philippians 1; others read "we" as "whoever of us is alive." The "word of the Lord" (4:15) may be an unrecorded saying of Jesus, a summary of the Gospel teaching, or a prophecy.
views.L: 4:1-12 is moral teaching in short commands; 4:13-18 has the shape of a consolation, from grief (4:13) to comfort (4:18). The descent of the Lord and the ascent of believers are told in a mirror pattern.
views.J: Jewish law and teaching on sexual holiness (Leviticus 18-20) lie behind 4:3-8. The trumpet, the archangel and the clouds come from Israel's Scriptures (Exodus 19:16; Daniel 7:13; Daniel 12:1-2). The hope of the resurrection of the dead was held by many Jews of Paul's day, the Pharisees among them.
views.T: The Latin rapiemur (4:17) gave English "rapture." The idea of a separate coming of Christ to take the church before a time of tribulation was taught by John Nelson Darby from about the 1830s (some date his first statement of it to 1827) and spread through the Scofield Reference Bible (1909); the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Reformed churches read the passage as part of Christ's one return. In Orthodox worship 4:13-17 is the Epistle read at funerals.

deep.b:
The Thessalonians did not ask Paul for a chart of the end. Their question came from a funeral: what happens to believers who die before the Lord comes? Paul's answer has three parts. Jesus died and rose, so those who die in him will rise (4:14). The dead have no disadvantage: they rise first (4:15-16). And all, the risen dead and the living together, will "be with the Lord always" (4:17). The details (the shout, the archangel, the trumpet, the clouds, the air) come from the language Jews and Christians used for God's coming, and Paul does not explain them.

Paul does not say here where the meeting leads. Two pictures have been drawn from the word apantesis, "meeting." On the first, believers go up like a city's leading citizens going out to meet an arriving ruler, and then come back with him to earth; John Chrysostom already used this picture (Homily 8 on 1 Thessalonians). On the second, believers are taken up to be with the Lord, and the picture of a civic welcome does not fit (Michael Cosby, 1994, with Robert Gundry's reply, 1996; Joseph Plevnik, 1999). The first fits readings in which Christ returns to reign on earth; the second fits readings in which believers are taken to heaven, either for a time (as in pre-tribulation teaching) or for good.

What the passage shows clearly is its purpose: "So comfort one another with these words" (4:18).

deep.h: Where the rapture teaching came from
deep.b: The verb "caught up" (harpazo) is rendered rapiemur, "we will be snatched up," in the Latin Vulgate, and from that verb comes the English word "rapture." For most of church history the event was read as part of Christ's one return at the end. From about the 1830s John Nelson Darby, a leader of the Plymouth Brethren, taught that Christ would first come for his church, taking believers out of the world before a time of tribulation, and later come with them. The Scofield Reference Bible (1909) spread this view widely, and it is common among Baptists in the United States, Pentecostals and non-denominational evangelicals. The Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran churches, and many Reformed churches, are amillennial: they expect no thousand-year reign on earth before the end and no separate coming before Christ's one return. Other premillennial Christians place the rapture in the middle of the tribulation, before God's wrath late in it (the pre-wrath view), or after it, at Christ's visible return (George Ladd, Douglas Moo). The card on this page sets the churches' teaching side by side.

echoes: Leviticus 18:24; Leviticus 19:2; Acts 15:29; Ezekiel 36:27; Ezekiel 37:14; Isaiah 54:13; Jeremiah 31:34; Daniel 12:1-2; Exodus 19:16; Daniel 7:13; Matthew 24:30-31; 1 Corinthians 15:51-52; 1 Corinthians 15:20-23; Acts 1:9-11; Acts 28:15; Matthew 25:6; John 11:11-14; 2 Thessalonians 2:1; 2 Thessalonians 3:6-12

settings.by: Paul and his co-workers, recalling the orders they gave "through the Lord Jesus" (4:2)
settings.to: The church at Thessalonica: mostly Gentile converts who had turned from the city's gods (1:9), with perhaps some Jews and God-fearers from the synagogue (Acts 17:4); working people for the most part (4:11), a few months old, meeting in houses, and under pressure from neighbors
settings.when: the same occasion; the teaching repeats what was given in person
settings.why: To hold Gentile converts to the standard of Israel's God in sexual conduct, where the customs of a Greek city allowed men much more. Paul ties holiness to God's will, God's call and the gift of the Spirit, not only to rules. The command binds every member, and the words "his own vessel" and "his brother" show that Paul is speaking first to the men. Knowing the audience changes the reading: this is not a general lecture but a hard change of life for people raised in another moral world.
views: "Vessel" is the man's own body: he must learn self-control.
"Vessel" is a wife: each man should take a wife of his own in a holy way, not seek sex outside marriage.
"Vessel" is a polite word for the man's own sexual organ: he must keep it under control.

settings.what: Love among brothers, and quiet work
settings.to: The church at Thessalonica: mostly Gentile converts who had turned from the city's gods (1:9), with perhaps some Jews and God-fearers from the synagogue (Acts 17:4); working people for the most part (4:11), a few months old, meeting in houses, and under pressure from neighbors
settings.why: To praise the church's love, already known across Macedonia, and to steer it: love should not become dependence, and zeal should not become disorder. Quiet work keeps the church able to help others and gives outsiders no cause for complaint. Knowing the audience changes the reading: these were mostly working people, some perhaps tempted to stop work or to live off others, in a city that had already rioted once over them.
views: Some had stopped working because they expected the Lord soon (compare 2 Thessalonians 3:6-12).
Some poorer members were living as clients of richer believers or patrons; Paul wants each to support himself.

settings.what: Comfort about those who have died
settings.by: Paul and his co-workers, citing "the Lord's word" (4:15)
settings.to: The church at Thessalonica: mostly Gentile converts who had turned from the city's gods (1:9), with perhaps some Jews and God-fearers from the synagogue (Acts 17:4); working people for the most part (4:11), a few months old, meeting in houses, and under pressure from neighbors
settings.when: after some members had died since the founding of the church
settings.why: To comfort grieving believers who feared that their dead would miss the Lord's coming, or who did not know that the dead in Christ would rise. Paul gives them words to say to one another at the graveside. Knowing the audience changes the reading: the passage answers a pastoral question, not a question about the timing of events, and its last word is comfort.
views: Paul's short stay left no time to teach about the resurrection of believers.
Feared the dead would miss out
They knew of the resurrection but feared those who died before the coming would lose their place at it.

traditions.q: Is the meeting "in the air" (4:17) a rapture of the church before the tribulation, or part of Christ's one return?
views: A separate event before the tribulation. Dallas Theological Seminary's Doctrinal Statement calls "the coming of the Lord in the air" to gather living and dead believers "the blessed hope," and teaches that this "translation of the church will be followed by the fulfillment of Israel's seventieth week" (articles 18-19).

The Assemblies of God, one of the largest Pentecostal bodies, calls the rising of those who have fallen asleep in Christ and their catching up together with the living the church's "imminent and blessed hope," followed by Christ's visible return and his thousand-year reign (Statement of Fundamental Truths, 13-14). Other Pentecostal churches have their own statements.

Divided. Many hold the pre-tribulation view; others place the rapture in the middle of the tribulation (Harold Ockenga, James Buswell), before God's wrath late in it (pre-wrath), or at Christ's one visible return after it (George Ladd, Douglas Moo, John Piper).

The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article 10) teaches that "Jesus Christ will return personally and visibly in glory to the earth" and does not fix the order of events. The pre-tribulation view is common among Baptists in the United States, but Baptists are divided.

One coming of Christ in glory, before which "the Church must pass through a final trial that will shake the faith of many believers" (Catechism 675); the Church "will enter the glory of the kingdom only through this final Passover" (677). The Catechism quotes 4:16 for the time of the resurrection: "at the last day," "at the end of the world," at Christ's coming (1001).

Part of Christ's one Second Coming, not a separate event before a tribulation: "The verse refers to something that will happen as part of the Lord's Coming." With Chrysostom, rising to meet him gives the descending King an escort. So the Orthodox priest Dimitri Cozby in a missionary leaflet, The Rapture (2001); it is one priest's statement, not a council's.

"At the Consummation of the World Christ will appear for judgment, and will raise up all the dead" (Augsburg Confession 17). The confession knows one appearing, and it rejects the teaching that the godly will take over the kingdoms of the world before the resurrection of the dead.

Christ comes once, on a day of judgment that God keeps unknown "that they may shake off all carnal security, and be always watchful" (Westminster Confession 33.3). The confession does not discuss 4:17 by name.

traditions.q: Those who have "fallen asleep" (4:13-15): are the dead in Christ conscious with the Lord before the resurrection, and may the living pray for them?
views: Yes. At death each soul is judged at once, "either entrance into the blessedness of heaven-through a purification or immediately," or damnation (Catechism 1022). Those "still imperfectly purified" undergo the purification the Church calls purgatory, and the Church prays for the dead, above all in the Eucharist (1030-1032). The body rises at Christ's return.

Yes. In Orthodox dogmatic theology the soul, after a particular judgment, has a foretaste of the blessedness or the torment that awaits it after the resurrection. The Church prays for the departed, asking God to "give rest to the souls of Thy departed servants in a place of brightness" (the Orthodox prayer for the departed).

At death "the souls of the righteous, being then made perfect in holiness, are received into the highest heavens," and "Besides these two places for souls separated from their bodies, the Scripture acknowledgeth none" (Westminster Confession 32.1). John Calvin taught that the dead are conscious while they await the Judgment.

"Until that day death is an unconscious state for all people"; when Christ appears, the righteous dead are raised and, with the living righteous, glorified (Seventh-day Adventist Fundamental Belief 26). Paul's "asleep" is taken at its word.

title: Children of the Day
sum: About the times and seasons, the church already knows enough: the day of the Lord will come like a thief at night, and ruin will fall on those who say "Peace and safety" (5:1-3). But believers belong to the day. They must stay awake and clear-headed, dressed in faith, love and hope, because God has appointed them not for anger but for salvation through the Lord Jesus, who died so that, alive or dead, they will live with him (5:4-11).

The letter ends with short commands for church life: respect those who lead, keep peace, help the weak, never repay evil for evil, rejoice always, pray without a break, give thanks, do not snuff out the Spirit or scorn prophecy, but test everything (5:12-22). A last prayer asks God to make them holy "spirit and soul and body" for Christ's coming, and Paul puts them under oath to read the letter to all (5:23-28).
readings: Ready, not anxious
Read as pastoral teaching, 5:1-11 tells believers not to calculate dates but to live as people of the day, so that the coming will find them ready whenever it comes.
A church under the empire
Read against Rome, the warning about "Peace and safety" may target the empire's claim to have brought peace and security, a claim the day of the Lord will expose (see the note at 5:3).

views.H: Rome boasted of bringing peace (pax), and some scholars hear that boast in "Peace and safety" (5:3). A church without titles relied on householders and hard workers as leaders (5:12).
views.C: Some have proposed that 5:1-11 was added later as a correction to 4:13-18; most see it as Paul's own continuation, since 5:10 picks up 4:14-17. The triad of faith, love and hope (5:8) links the passage to 1:3.
views.L: 5:1-11 is built on contrasts: night and day, darkness and light, sleep and waking, drunk and sober, anger and salvation. 5:16-22 is a string of very short commands, almost a rule of life.
views.J: "The day of the Lord" is the prophets' phrase (Amos 5:18; Joel 2:1). "Sons of light" is a Jewish idiom known from the Dead Sea Scrolls' War Scroll. The armor of 5:8 is God's armor in Isaiah 59:17. The holy kiss and the oath by the Lord (5:26-27) mark a community that sees itself as a family bound before God.
views.T: "Pray without a break" (5:17) shaped Augustine's teaching on prayer as desire and the Orthodox practice of the Jesus Prayer. The Catholic Catechism cites 5:12 and 5:19-21 on testing the gifts of the Spirit (801) and 5:23 on soul and spirit (367).

deep.b: Paul prays that God will keep the readers' "spirit and soul and body" whole and blameless (5:23). Since Irenaeus in the second century, who quoted this verse in Against Heresies (book 5, chapter 6), Christians have asked whether it describes three parts of a human being. Those who say yes (trichotomists) distinguish the spirit, which relates to God, from the soul, the seat of mind and feeling, and the body. Those who say no (dichotomists) see a human being as body and soul, and read Paul's three words as a way of saying "all of you," like "heart, being, mind and strength" in the great commandment. The Reformed theologian Louis Berkhof wrote that this verse and Hebrews 4:12 "do not prove the point." The Catholic Catechism (367) cites this verse and says, "The Church teaches that this distinction does not introduce a duality into the soul": "spirit" means that a person is made for a supernatural end, communion with God. The verse's own concern is wholeness: nothing in the person left out of God's work of making holy.
deep.refs: 1 Thessalonians 5:23; Hebrews 4:12; Genesis 2:7; Mark 12:30; 1 Corinthians 2:14-15; Matthew 10:28

deep.title: Claude's theory: the letter's last half is a syllabus built from 3:10
deep.b: In 3:10 Paul prays to "make up what is still missing in your faith." In 3:6 Timothy's report names their faith and their love, but not their hope, though 1:3 named all three. Chapters 4 and 5 can be read as a short course on what was missing: holiness and love, which they had but needed to grow in (4:1-12), and above all hope, for the dead (4:13-18) and for the day (5:1-11), ending with the triad restored as armor (5:8). If so, the letter's structure is the answer to Timothy's report. Many commentators link 3:10 with chapters 4-5; the point about hope's absence from 3:6 is the part offered here as Claude's suggestion, and it rests on an argument from silence.

echoes: Acts 1:7; Daniel 2:21; Amos 5:18; Joel 2:1; Joel 2:31; Matthew 24:43; Luke 12:39; Revelation 3:3; Revelation 16:15; Jeremiah 6:14; Jeremiah 8:11; Isaiah 13:8; Matthew 24:8; John 12:36; Romans 13:11-13; Isaiah 59:17; Ephesians 6:14-17; Romans 12:17; 1 Corinthians 14:29; Romans 16:16; Romans 16:20; 2 Thessalonians 3:16-18

settings.to: The church at Thessalonica: mostly Gentile converts who had turned from the city's gods (1:9), with perhaps some Jews and God-fearers from the synagogue (Acts 17:4); working people for the most part (4:11), a few months old, meeting in houses, and under pressure from neighbors
settings.when: the same occasion, right after the comfort about the dead
settings.why: To calm a church that may have been anxious about when the day would come and whether it would catch them unready. Paul refuses to give dates and tells them instead who they are: people of the day, appointed for salvation. Knowing the audience changes the reading: the warnings about sudden ruin are aimed at outsiders who trust in false peace; to the church Paul speaks comfort (5:11).
views: The church had asked, or Paul expected them to ask, when the day would come.
Paul warns against the empire's or the city's confidence in its own peace and security.

settings.to: The same church, all its members, with first words about those who lead them
settings.why: To give a young church without titled officers a few rules that would hold it together: respect for those who work and lead, care for the disorderly, the timid and the weak, no revenge, joy, prayer and thanks, and a balanced view of prophecy: welcome it, test it. Knowing the audience changes the reading: these commands are not timeless proverbs only; each answers a need in a small church under pressure.

settings.by: Paul and his co-workers, with Paul taking an oath in his own voice (5:27)
settings.to: The church at Thessalonica: mostly Gentile converts who had turned from the city's gods (1:9), with perhaps some Jews and God-fearers from the synagogue (Acts 17:4); working people for the most part (4:11), a few months old, meeting in houses, and under pressure from neighbors
settings.why: To end with a prayer for complete holiness at the Lord's coming, ask for the church's prayers, send the holy kiss, and make sure every believer hears the letter read. Knowing the audience changes the reading: the oath suggests the church met in more than one house, or that Paul feared his words might not reach everyone.

traditions.q: "Do not snuff out the Spirit. Do not treat prophecies as nothing" (5:19-20): do gifts such as prophecy continue, and who tests them?
views: The Spirit's charisms continue as graces that build up the Church, and charity is their measure. Citing this passage (5:12, 19-21), the Catechism teaches that discernment belongs to the Church's pastors: "No charism is exempt from being referred and submitted to the Church's shepherds" (Catechism 799-801).

The gifts continue. The Assemblies of God teaches the baptism in the Holy Spirit as "a separate and subsequent experience following conversion," with speaking in tongues as its "initial physical evidence" (Statement of Fundamental Truths, 7-8).

Divided. Many follow the Westminster Confession's statement that "those former ways of God's revealing His will unto His people" are "now ceased" (1.1), so prophecy in the sense of new revelation has ended. Some Reformed teachers are continuationists.

The miraculous signs given through apostles and prophets "ceased with the passing of these foundational offices," and speaking in tongues was never "the common or necessary mark" of the Spirit's baptism (Dallas Theological Seminary, Doctrinal Statement, article 16).
